items: Apply organisation schemes, labelling and navigation systems
Choose between card sorting, tree testing and first-click testing
See where IA hides inside retrieval-augmented systems

reading.text: Information architecture is the structural work that decides whether anything can be found. It is largely invisible when done well, which is why it is under-resourced, and it is the first thing that fails as a product accumulates features.
The four systems
Core IA (Rosenfeld, Morville & Arango, Information Architecture, 4th ed. 2015) works through four systems: organisation schemes, labelling, navigation, and search.

Organisation schemes divide into exact and ambiguous. Exact schemes — alphabetical, chronological, geographical — are unambiguous, need no judgement, and are useful only when the user already knows the item's name, date or place. Ambiguous schemes — by topic, by task, by audience — require someone to decide what goes where, and they are the ones that make a site usable for people who do not yet know what they are looking for. They are also where all the arguments happen, because ambiguous means genuinely debatable.

Labelling is the surface of the organisation scheme and carries most of its usability. Navigation divides into global, which is present everywhere and defines the space; local, which shows where you are within a branch; and contextual, which links sideways from inside content. Search is the fourth system rather than an escape hatch from the other three, and treating it as a substitute for structure produces sites where nothing can be browsed.
How people actually search

Bates' berry-picking model (1989) describes real search behaviour better than classic information retrieval: the need evolves as you learn, and the query changes with it. Teevan et al. (CHI 2004) contrast orienteering — navigating in small steps from a known point — with teleporting, jumping directly to the target.

Classic IR models a fixed information need matched against a corpus. Berry-picking says the need is not fixed: each partial find changes what you are looking for, so the search is a path through an evolving question rather than a single lookup. That is why search results pages need to support reformulation rather than only ranking.

The orienteering finding is the one that surprises designers. People often navigate in small confident steps from a known starting point even when a direct search would be faster — because each step confirms they are still in the right place, and a search that fails leaves them nowhere. Structure keeps earning its keep even in a system with excellent search.
Methods

Methods: open and closed card sorting, analysed by clustering the similarity matrix; tree testing for findability isolated from visual design; and first-click testing — getting the first click right roughly doubles task success (Sauro).

The three answer different questions and are often confused. An open card sort asks users to group items and name the groups, which generates candidate structure. A closed sort gives them your categories and asks where items belong, which validates a structure you already have. Tree testing strips away all visual design and asks where someone would look in the bare hierarchy — so a failure is unambiguously structural rather than a styling problem.

First-click testing is the cheapest of the four and has the starkest result. If the first click is right, task success roughly doubles; if it is wrong, users rarely recover, because recovering means admitting the model they formed was wrong and starting again. That makes the top-level labels disproportionately important relative to everything beneath them.
Ontology and taxonomy: controlled vocabularies and faceted classification, from Ranganathan's legacy through to faceted search (Hearst, Search User Interfaces, 2009).

Facets are the practical descendant of that lineage. Rather than forcing one hierarchy, faceted classification describes items along several independent dimensions — material, price, colour, era — and lets the user compose the path. It works because it does not require the designer to guess which dimension matters most to a given person on a given day.
IA in the LLM era

Conversational retrieval collapses navigation into query reformulation, and RAG systems reintroduce IA invisibly — chunking is a taxonomy decision users never see. "Citations as navigation" is the emerging pattern.

The invisibility is the problem worth naming. When a corpus is split into chunks and indexed, someone has decided what belongs together and what is separable — which is a classification decision in every meaningful sense. It determines what can be retrieved as a unit and therefore what the system can answer well, and no user will ever see the scheme or be able to tell that a bad answer came from a bad split.

Citations as navigation is the partial remedy: if the answer names its sources and those names are followable, the user regains something like contextual navigation — a way to move sideways out of an answer into the material behind it, which is exactly what the fourth IA system was for.

items: Rosenfeld, Morville & Arango, Information Architecture (4th ed. 2015)
Bates, the berry-picking model (1989)
Teevan et al., orienteering versus teleporting (CHI 2004)
Hearst, Search User Interfaces (2009)

reading.text: Card-sort your own portfolio's project set with eight participants. Compare the resulting clusters to your current site sections.

cards.back: Orienteering: navigating in small steps from a known starting point. Teleporting: jumping directly to the target via search. Users orienteer more than designers expect.
Real search is an evolving series of partial finds where the query changes as you learn, not a single matched retrieval against a fixed need.

cards.front: Tree testing — what does it isolate?
cards.back: Findability of the structure itself, stripped of visual design, by asking users where they would look in a bare hierarchy.
Users who get the first click right succeed at roughly double the rate of those who do not.

cards.front: Where does IA hide in a RAG system?
cards.back: In chunking and retrieval structure — a taxonomy decision made by engineers that users never see but always feel.

quiz.question: You want to know whether your category structure works, independent of visual design. Which method?
quiz.why: Tree testing presents the bare hierarchy with no layout or styling, isolating structure. Card sorting generates structure rather than validating it.

quiz.question: In what sense does a RAG pipeline make an IA decision?
options: Chunking and retrieval boundaries are an invisible taxonomy that determines what can be found
It applies a controlled vocabulary to user queries
It does not — retrieval is purely statistical
quiz.why: How documents are split and indexed decides what is retrievable together. That is a classification decision with no user-facing surface.

lessons.title: Visual Design: Gestalt, Typography, Hierarchy, Motion

items: Use Gestalt grouping deliberately rather than decoratively
Engineer scan order through visual hierarchy
Treat design systems as encoded HCI research

reading.text: Visual design in an interface is not decoration applied after the structure is decided. It is the mechanism by which structure becomes perceivable — which means a layout either communicates the organisation you built or contradicts it, and there is no neutral option.
Gestalt grouping

Gestalt principles (the Wertheimer 1923 lineage): proximity, similarity, continuity, closure, common region and common fate. Proximity and common region do most of the work in interface layout — grouping by whitespace beats boxes and rules, because it adds less extraneous load.

The principles describe how the visual system assembles parts into wholes before you have consciously read anything. Things near each other are taken as belonging together; things that look alike are taken as the same kind; things enclosed by a boundary form a unit; things that move together are one object. None of that requires attention, which is why layout communicates faster than labels.

The practical ranking matters. Proximity groups without adding any marks at all — you move things closer and the relationship appears free. Common region groups by enclosure, which works but adds a border the reader must also process. Given a choice, spend space rather than ink: the whitespace version costs the reader nothing to decode, and the boxed version adds an element that competes with the content it was meant to organise.

That is also the diagnostic for over-designed interfaces. If a layout needs boxes, rules, tints and three weights to explain itself, the underlying grouping is usually unclear rather than under-decorated, and adding marks is treating the symptom.
Typography
Typography: hierarchy comes from size, weight and spacing; line length runs around 45–75 characters; and on-screen legibility is driven by contrast and x-height.

The measure figure is the one most often violated by responsive layouts, because a column that simply fills the viewport will run to a hundred characters or more on a wide screen. Long lines make the return sweep a search: the eye has to find the start of the next line, and the further it travels the more often it lands wrong. Leading is chosen against the measure rather than independently — a wider column needs more space between lines to keep the horizontal channel findable.

X-height and contrast matter more on screen than in print because rendering is coarser and viewing conditions are worse. A typeface with a large x-height carries more legibility at small sizes than its nominal point size suggests, which is why a 15px face can outperform a 16px one.
Visual hierarchy is engineered scan order, built from size, contrast, position and whitespace. F- and Z-pattern findings are eyetracking descriptions of particular layouts, not laws to design toward.

That correction is worth holding onto. The F-pattern was observed on text-heavy pages with weak hierarchy — it describes what people do when nothing is guiding them. Treating it as a template inverts cause and effect: design a strong hierarchy and the scan path follows it instead.
Motion

Motion: functional animation supports object constancy and perceived causality (the cartoon-animation-in-UI lineage, Chang & Ungar, UIST 1993); 200–500 ms is typical; and `prefers-reduced-motion` must be respected, because vestibular disorders make gratuitous motion genuinely harmful.

Object constancy is the useful concept. When an element moves rather than disappearing and reappearing, the viewer tracks it as the same thing in a new place — so a transition can answer "where did that go?" without a word. Perceived causality is the companion: motion that begins where the user acted reads as a consequence of the action rather than an unrelated event.

That gives a clean test for whether an animation earns its place. If it tells the viewer where something went or what caused what, it is doing work. If it exists to feel polished, it is spending attention — and for users with vestibular disorders it can cause real nausea and dizziness, which is why the reduced-motion setting is a health accommodation rather than a taste preference.

Design systems — Material, Apple HIG, Fluent, Carbon, Polaris — encode tokens, components and patterns for consistency at organisational scale. Study them as compiled HCI research rather than as style guides.

Read that way, a design system's specifications are findings rather than opinions: minimum touch target sizes are Fitts and motor precision, contrast floors are perception and accessibility research, motion durations come from the object-constancy work. The system is a delivery mechanism for evidence, which is also why departing from one should be a considered decision rather than an aesthetic reflex.

items: Wertheimer and the Gestalt lineage (1923 onward)
Butterick, Practical Typography; Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style
Chang & Ungar, animation in user interfaces (UIST 1993)
Material, Apple HIG, Fluent, Carbon, Polaris

reading.text: Take one of your project pages and produce three variants manipulating only whitespace and type scale. Test scan order with a five-second test on six peers.

cards.front: Which Gestalt principles carry most of the load in UI layout?
cards.back: Proximity and common region. Grouping by whitespace beats drawing boxes and rules, because it adds less extraneous load.
Roughly 45–75 characters. Longer lines cost the reader accurate return sweeps.
Engineered scan order, produced by size, contrast, position and whitespace.
An eyetracking description of how people scanned particular text-heavy layouts — not a law, and not a template to design toward.
Object constancy and perceived causality — the viewer can see where a thing went and what caused it. Typical durations run 200–500 ms.

quiz.question: Two related fields need to read as a group. Which is the better first move?
options: Draw a bordered box around them
Reduce the space between them and increase the space around them
Give them the same background tint
quiz.why: Proximity groups without adding marks. Boxes, tints and headings all work, but each adds visual elements the reader must process.

quiz.question: Why must interfaces honour prefers-reduced-motion?
options: Motion can trigger genuine vestibular symptoms, so it is an accessibility requirement rather than a preference
It is required by WCAG level AAA only
quiz.why: For users with vestibular disorders, parallax and large transitions can cause nausea and dizziness. The setting is a health accommodation.

exact.prompt: Typical duration range for functional animation, in milliseconds
exact.note: Functional animation supports object constancy and perceived causality (Chang & Ungar, UIST 1993). Outside this range it reads as either a glitch or a wait.

items: Apply the WCAG baseline correctly
Distinguish inclusive, universal and ability-based design
See AI as both assistive technology and new barrier

reading.text: Accessibility is the part of interface design with an actual legal floor, which makes it unusual: most of this book offers evidence you can weigh, and this chapter offers requirements you meet or fail. It is also the part where a compliance mindset produces the worst outcomes, because passing an automated check and being usable by a disabled person are different achievements.
The baseline

WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation, 2023) organises everything under four POUR principles — Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust — at conformance levels A, AA and AAA. Regionally: EN 301 549 in the EU, the ADA and Section 508 in the US, IS 5568 in Israel. WCAG 3.0 remains in draft.

The four principles are worth reading as a sequence of failure modes rather than categories. Perceivable: can the person receive the information at all, through whichever senses they have. Operable: can they drive the interface, with whatever input they use. Understandable: can they make sense of the content and the behaviour. Robust: will it keep working with assistive technology as both evolve.

AA is the level nearly all legislation targets, and it is the practical bar. AAA contains criteria that are genuinely unreasonable for some content types, which is why the standard itself does not recommend AAA conformance across a whole site.

Assistive technology: screen readers, driven by semantic HTML and ARIA — the first rule of ARIA is do not use ARIA when native semantics exist — plus switch access, magnification, captions and voice control.

The first rule of ARIA is the single most useful thing in this chapter for anyone writing markup. A native `button` arrives with keyboard activation, focus behaviour, the correct role and the correct state reporting, all free and all correct. A `div` with `role="button"` has the role and nothing else, so you now owe the keyboard handler, the focus management and the state — and you will get one of them wrong.

The other technologies are worth knowing because they fail differently. Switch access depends entirely on a sane focus order, since the user moves through elements sequentially with no ability to jump. Magnification depends on reflow, because a user at 400% zoom sees a fraction of the layout at a time. Voice control depends on visible labels matching accessible names, since the user says what they see.
Beyond compliance

Inclusive design and Microsoft's persona spectrum — permanent, temporary and situational disability; universal design (Mace); and ability-based design (Wobbrock et al., TACCESS 2011), which adapts systems to the abilities a user has rather than requiring users to adapt to the system.

The persona spectrum is the argument that moves budgets. One arm can mean an amputation, a broken wrist, or holding a baby; low vision can mean a permanent condition, an eye infection, or sunlight on a screen. The same accommodation serves all three, which reframes accessibility work from a small fixed population to a large intermittent one — most people are situationally disabled regularly.

Ability-based design inverts the usual framing more sharply. Rather than asking what a user cannot do and providing a workaround, it asks what they can do and builds the interaction from that — which produces different designs rather than adapted ones.
Cognitive accessibility — plain language, consistent navigation, error tolerance — is chronically under-implemented relative to sensory accessibility.

Part of the reason is that it resists automated checking. A tool can measure contrast and detect a missing label; nothing can measure whether a sentence is comprehensible or whether an error message tells someone what to do next. So the work that is easy to verify gets done and the work that requires judgement does not, despite affecting a larger population.
AI in both directions

AI cuts both ways: as assistive technology — scene description, live captioning, voice control for motor impairments, as in the Be My Eyes deployments — and as a new barrier, through unlabelled generated UI and hallucinated image descriptions. Both are live research areas at ASSETS and CHI.

The assistive gains are real and large: a system that describes a photograph, reads a menu aloud or captions a meeting live does something no previous technology could. The barrier is subtler and worth stating precisely. A hallucinated image description is confidently wrong in a channel the user cannot cross-check — a sighted person can glance at the picture and catch the error, and the person relying on the description cannot. Confident wrongness is worse than silence for exactly the population that has no second channel.
Checklist

items: Contrast at least 4.5:1 for body text
Full keyboard operability with a visible focus indicator
Targets at least 24 × 24 CSS pixels (WCAG 2.2)
Never encode by colour alone
Captions plus transcripts
Test with an actual screen reader, not only an automated auditor

reading.text: The last line carries the others. Automated tools catch a minority of real barriers — the machine-checkable subset — and a clean report says only that nothing in that subset failed. Focus order, label quality, whether the reading sequence makes sense, whether an interaction is completable without a mouse: all of that needs a person and the actual assistive technology.

items: Wobbrock et al., Ability-Based Design (2011, TACCESS, DOI 10.1145/1952383.1952384)
Mace, universal design
Microsoft Inclusive Design, the persona spectrum

reading.text: Navigate your portfolio site using only a keyboard, then with VoiceOver or NVDA. Log every trap and fix the worst three.

cards.back: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust — the four WCAG principles.
Do not use ARIA when native HTML semantics already provide the role and behaviour. Native elements come with keyboard and screen-reader support already correct.
Disability as permanent, temporary or situational — one arm, a broken arm, holding a baby. It widens who a given accommodation serves.
Wobbrock et al. (2011): adapt the system to the abilities the user has, rather than requiring the user to adapt to the system.
Body text contrast at least 4.5:1; target size at least 24 × 24 CSS pixels.

cards.front: How is AI a new accessibility barrier?
cards.back: Generated UI arrives unlabelled and unstructured, and hallucinated image descriptions are confidently wrong in a channel the user cannot cross-check.

quiz.question: A component needs a button role. What is the correct approach?
options: A div with role="button" and a keydown handler
A span with aria-label and tabindex
Either, as long as ARIA is present
quiz.why: The first rule of ARIA: prefer native semantics. A real button brings focus, keyboard activation and screen-reader role for free, with nothing to reimplement or get wrong.

quiz.question: An automated auditor reports zero accessibility errors. What can you conclude?
options: Only that a subset of machine-checkable rules passed; keyboard and screen-reader testing is still required
The product meets AA but not AAA
quiz.why: Automated tools catch a minority of real barriers. Focus order, label quality and screen-reader coherence need manual testing with the actual assistive technology.

quiz.question: Which accessibility area does the book call chronically under-implemented?
quiz.why: Plain language, consistent navigation and error tolerance receive far less attention than sensory accommodations, despite affecting a large population.

exact.prompt: Which WCAG conformance level does nearly all legislation target?
exact.note: A and AAA exist, but AA is the practical bar — it is what the law asks for and what this app's own contrast checks are measured against.

exact.prompt: In what year did WCAG 2.2 become a W3C Recommendation?
exact.note: It organises everything under the four POUR principles — Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.

items: Rank visual encodings by decoding accuracy
Apply the visual information-seeking mantra
Connect uncertainty visualisation to AI confidence display

reading.text: Data visualisation is the one area of interface design with a genuine experimental ranking of techniques. That makes it unusual and useful: many of its choices can be settled by evidence rather than argued from taste.
Graphical perception

Cleveland & McGill (1984, JASA) ranked encodings by how accurately people decode quantity from them: position beats length, which beats angle, which beats area, which beats colour. This is the empirical basis for "bar beats pie".

The experiment behind the ranking is worth knowing because it is what makes the claim more than an opinion. Participants were shown values encoded different ways and asked to judge ratios; the error rates ordered the channels. So the ranking is not about which chart looks better but about how wrong people are when they read it.

The pie chart follows directly. A pie encodes by angle and area — two channels near the bottom of the ranking — while a bar chart encodes by position along a common scale and by length, the top two. That is why a pie can be beautiful and still leave the reader unable to tell which of two similar slices is larger.

The ranking also tells you when a weaker channel is acceptable. If the reader only needs to see that one value is dramatically larger, area will do. If they need to compare precisely, or to rank several similar values, you have to spend position and length on it. The question is always what judgement the reader must make, not which chart type is fashionable.
Tufte's principles — data-ink ratio, chartjunk — are useful heuristics, some of them contested. Bertin's Semiology of Graphics (1967) is the more systematic foundation.

Tufte's rules are memorable and have been genuinely useful, and parts have not held up under testing — the strongest versions of the chartjunk argument have been challenged by studies finding that some decoration aids recall without harming accuracy. Treat them as heuristics that usually point the right way rather than as findings. Bertin's work is the deeper foundation: a systematic account of the visual variables and what each can encode.
Interaction
Shneiderman's visual information-seeking mantra (1996): overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand.

The sequence is a design order, not a menu. Overview first, because a reader who cannot see the shape of the whole cannot form a question worth asking. Zoom and filter next, so they can narrow to the region their question is about. Details on demand last, because detail shown before it is wanted is noise, and detail unavailable when wanted is a dead end.
Uncertainty

Uncertainty visualisation (Hullman, Kay and colleagues): hypothetical outcome plots and quantile dotplots communicate uncertainty better than error bars or bare percentages. This feeds directly into AI confidence display.

The reason those forms outperform is that they replace an abstraction with something countable. An error bar asks the reader to reason about a distribution from a drawn interval, which people do badly and inconsistently. A quantile dotplot shows a set of discrete outcomes — nineteen dots here, one there — and frequency framings map onto how people actually reason about chance.
If a number will be read as certain when it is not, the visualisation has failed no matter how accurate the number is.

That is the bridge to the trust chapter. A model's "87% confident" is both miscalibrated and read as more precise than it is, which is the same failure in a different costume — a quantity presented in a form the reader will systematically over-trust.

items: Cleveland & McGill, Graphical perception (1984, JASA)
Bertin, Semiology of Graphics (1967)
Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
Shneiderman, The Eyes Have It (1996, IEEE VL)
Hullman, Kay et al., on uncertainty visualisation

cards.back: Position, then length, then angle, then area, then colour — ordered by how accurately people decode quantity from each.

cards.front: Why does a bar chart beat a pie chart?
cards.back: Bars encode by position and length, which people decode accurately. Pies encode by angle and area, which they decode poorly.
Overview first, zoom and filter, details on demand (Shneiderman 1996).

cards.front: Quantile dotplots and hypothetical outcome plots
cards.back: Frequency-framed uncertainty displays that let people reason about a distribution without decoding an abstract interval.

cards.front: How should Tufte's principles be treated?
cards.back: As useful heuristics, partly contested empirically — not as laws. Bertin is the more systematic foundation.

quiz.question: You must show five proportions that readers will compare precisely. Best encoding?
options: Bar chart with a common baseline
quiz.why: Position along a common scale plus length are the two most accurately decoded channels. Area and colour sit near the bottom of the ranking.

quiz.question: Why do quantile dotplots outperform a "73% confident" label?
options: They frame uncertainty as countable outcomes rather than an abstract number people systematically misread
quiz.why: Frequency framings map onto how people reason about chance. A bare percentage is read as a property of the answer rather than as a distribution.
